new_statements.quote: Das Ur-Ambon betonte alle mehr als einsilbigen Wörter auf der Pänultima des Grundwortes. [...] Eine vierte Gruppe hat den Ton gleichfalls nach dem Wortende zu gerückt, jedoch nur, weil sich dem Stützvokal noch ein weiteres einsilbiges Suffix anheftete. Hierher gehören die Sprachen von Amahei, Nusalaut und Saparua. [...] Die Nominalendung -lo, welche sich im Amahei, Saparua und Nusalaut jedem Präfix-Substantivum anheftet, beeinflußt die Lage des Akzentes nicht: Feuer SA. ápu(y) > Am. háu-ro, Spr., N. háu-lo [...] Ebbe SA. mĕti > Spr., N. móti-lo. Infolgedessen ist der Vokal des Suffixes im Nusalaut und Saparua meist verstummt: König SA. látu > Spr. látu-l, N. lá'u-l
new_statements.translation: Ur-Ambon stressed all words of more than one syllable on the penult of the base. [...] A fourth group has likewise moved the accent toward the end of the word, but only because a further monosyllabic suffix attached itself to the support vowel. To it belong the languages of Amahei, Nusalaut and Saparua. [...] The nominal ending -lo, which in Amahei, Saparua and Nusalaut attaches to every prefixed noun, does not affect the position of the accent: fire SA. ápu(y) > Am. háu-ro, Spr., N. háu-lo [...] ebb SA. mĕti > Spr., N. móti-lo. Consequently the vowel of the suffix has mostly become silent in Nusalaut and Saparua: king SA. látu > Spr. látu-l, N. lá'u-l

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the base (the inherited Ur-Ambon rule); the nominal ending -lo/-ljo is not counted, so a stem plus -lo is stressed on the stem penult (háu-lo, móti-lo) and the suffix vowel usually drops (lá'u-l, húwa-l, muláha-l, giving surface penult). Where a support vowel -o or a 3sg possessive -i stood between stem and -lo the accent moved one syllable rightward to the second stem syllable = the then antepenult (nuwól-lo < *nuwól-o-lo, urít-i-l), and verbal suffixes -e and -lo pull the accent onto the new penult (palá-e, tomá-lo, iló-lo). Net: penult of the suffixed word in most forms, with nominal -lo extrametrical. Corroborated by van Hoëvell 1877:13-14 (penultimate as a rule for the five dialects incl. Nusalaut, stressed vowel long; only Haruku and Asilulu deviate).
new_statements.exceptions: Stresemann: nominal -lo does not shift the accent (háu-lo, móti-lo = surface antepenult), but support vowel + -lo, possessive -i + -lo, and the verbal suffixes -e / -lo do shift it toward the word end; van Hoëvell 1877:12 notes changed stress between the Saparua/Nusalaut -nno/-llo forms and the Haruku/Hila/Asilulu -no/-ne forms; van Hoëvell's stated exceptions to penult stress are Haruku and Asilulu, not Nusalaut.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited citation forms of c. 1910-12 (Stresemann's own Nusalaut material, Nalahia village 'N.'; Amet 'NA.' not cited in the stress section); historical-comparative monograph organised by sound change, not a synchronic phonology. van Hoëvell 1877 is a wordlist introduction covering five dialects jointly.
new_statements.identity_note: Stresemann 1927 distinguishes two Nusalaut varieties: 'N.' = Nusalaut (Nalahia village) — the variety cited in § 177 — and 'NA.' = Nusalaut (Amet), which retains *t (Collins 1983 fn. 167); the stress section cites only 'N.'. van Hoëvell 1877's Nusalaut column is unlocalised (he notes Amet keeps t where the rest of the island drops it). Both fall under Glottolog nusa1245 (no dialect-level codes); Kotynski/Travis 1989 wordlist site is Titawae. The language is dormant (10 speakers 1989, extinct c. 2000), so no modern instrumental or synchronic description exists.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work was listed (Kotynski 1989) and it was opened and confirmed silent. As extra spot-checks I searched the other saved silent sources in the same directory: Collins 1983 (PL-D47) has 19 stress/accent lines but none within three lines of 'Nusa'/'Nusalaut' (its only explicit stress rules are Hoamoal vs Asilulu, p. 82); Stokhof 1982 (PL-D50) has only the editorial 'Parts of words are sometimes underlined; stress?' (sec. 1.2.2, Abubu list, p. 91) and no rule; Travis 1989 has no stress/accent/penult hits and mentions Nusa Laut only as 'TITAWAE (Nusa Laut)' in its matrix and 'NUSALAUT (dying)' in the West Seram survey's language list. Nothing missed.

sources.note: No statement on Nusalaut stress. Nusalaut only in subgrouping (East Piru Bay: Saparua-Nusalaut-Amahai, pp. 85-98; van Hoëvell 1877:12 and Stresemann 1927:100 cited for -llo/-nno, r vs l and *t loss except in Amet, fn. 167) and comparative tables.
